steps.text: Explore the Serra do Caramulo in central Portugal, where the July 2026 wildfire began near Tourelhe.

layers.caption: This satellite image shows the hills and valleys of the Serra do Caramulo before the wildfire.

steps.text: Move the slider to see how two satellites show the same landscape.

layers.caption: This image uses reflected sunlight to show the landscape in natural colour.
In this radar image, brighter areas sent a stronger echo back to the satellite.

steps.text: The wildfire was reported near Tourelhe, in Vouzela, at 03:04 local time on 2 July 2026.

layers.caption: The Tourelhe marker locates the reported ignition area.

steps.text: During the wildfire, residents were evacuated from Matadegas and Mançores in Tondela.

layers.caption: The map locates the two communities reported evacuated.

steps.text: The fire was reported under control at 12:40 local time on 5 July 2026.

layers.caption: The map shows communities and landmarks associated with the fire.

steps.text: The wildfire burned through the Cambarinho Botanical Reserve.

layers.caption: The reserve marker is located at the start of the Cambarinho walking trail.

steps.text: Compare the radar measurements across the fire with those from the following 12 days.

layers.caption: Radar echoes were less similar between the two passes across a broad area on the northwestern slopes of the Serra do Caramulo, stretching from Tourelhe towards Águeda.
In the two passes after the fire, radar echoes were more similar across much of the same area.

steps.text: Use the official ICNF perimeter to see where the low-coherence pattern overlaps the mapped burned area.

layers.caption: This image shows where radar echoes were less similar between the passes on 29 June and 11 July.
The outline marks the area that Portugal’s forest agency, ICNF, mapped as burned.

steps.text: Compare two radar channels from the same overpass and look for areas that appear bright in one channel and dark in the other.

layers.caption: In this HH image, the radar sent and received waves in the same orientation.
In this HV image, the radar received echoes turned sideways, which can happen when waves scatter through branches and leaves.

steps.text: Radar brightness measures the strength of a return from one pass, while coherence measures how similar the radar signals were across two passes.

layers.caption: One possible reason some burned areas still appear bright is that standing trunks may continue to reflect radar waves.
Lower coherence shows where radar echoes were less alike between the two passes, which can indicate a change on the ground.

steps.text: Compare July and August radar returns to see which parts of the landscape changed after the fire.

layers.caption: The 11 July image shows the strength of the radar return shortly after the fire.
The 16 August image shows the radar return over the same landscape later in the summer.

steps.text: Compare coherence in July and October to see where the radar signals were more consistent between successive passes.

layers.caption: The July pair shows how similar the radar signals were during the first weeks after the fire.
The October pair shows how similar the radar signals were during a later 12-day period.

steps.text: Tondela and the University of Aveiro began preparing measures to address the effects of the fire in the Serra do Caramulo.

layers.caption: The ICNF perimeter gives a geographic reference for discussing post-fire recovery.

steps.text: Explore the available dates and layers, then follow the official perimeter to see where the radar pattern changes.

layers.caption: This coherence map provides a starting point for exploring the changes observed across the fire.
The ICNF outline helps you compare the radar signal inside and outside the mapped burned area.
